vars.proof: I'm doing this right now for a contractor in Arizona. Same problem: the work moves, but the status and the money don't.
vars.offerGoal: the top three places your jobs and your money are leaking
vars.offerWhy: I'm doing them now, before the snow, so whatever I find gets fixed before spring.
vars.tipFallback: start a 10-minute Monday review of every open job: what stage it's in, how long it's been there, and what money is still owed on it.

Insurance work: The insurance company's person who inspects damage and approves the claim. Desk adjuster = remote, field adjuster = on the roof.
The insurer's list of what they'll pay for.
The software insurers use to price claims, so roofers use it too.
A request for more money when the insurer's scope missed something. Often left open: big source of uncollected money.
Replacement cost value (the full amount) vs. actual cash value (paid up front, minus depreciation).
Money the insurer holds back until the job is done. The "depreciation check" often never gets collected.
Certificate of completion. Sent to the insurer to release the depreciation.
Insurance check made out to the homeowner AND the mortgage company. Needs both signatures; slow.
Overhead and profit (10% each) insurers sometimes add.
Extra work required by current building code, often supplemented.
The roof: 100 sq ft of roof. How roofs are measured and priced.
The wood boards under the shingles.
Layers under the shingles that keep water out.
Metal and vent parts at edges, walls and the peak.
The business: The install side (production manager, production schedule).
Homeowner pays directly vs. an insurance claim pays.
Out-of-town companies that follow hail storms.
How many roofers find leads after a storm.
Their software: Job-site photos, shared with the office.

guess.label: Make a guess
guess.title: Educated guesses: one at a time, then stop talking

guesses.ask: I'd bet you've got depreciation checks out there nobody's chased in a while. Am I wrong?
guesses.label: Depreciation not chased
guesses.tip: Find the recoverable-depreciation deadline in the policy on every open claim. It varies by carrier and policy, so don't guess it. Work the list by deadline, not by date finished, because a check past its deadline is just gone.
guesses.fix: Moving a job to Built creates a "send the completion paperwork" task (certificate of completion and final invoice) with that claim's deadline on it. The check sits on the money-owed list until it arrives, and the Friday review catches anything close to its deadline.

guesses.ask: When an inspection doesn't turn into a claim, does anyone follow up?
guesses.label: Inspections go nowhere
guesses.tip: Call back every inspection from this season that never filed, with the storm date. Policies have deadlines for reporting a claim, so it's a reason to call that isn't a sales pitch.
guesses.fix: Every inspection is a card on the board. One that doesn't file gets the same follow-ups as a quote (day 2, 5 and 10), then a follow-up date that brings it back before the season ends.

guesses.ask: When you're all up on roofs, who answers the phone?
guesses.label: Missed calls on job days
guesses.tip: Call your own number from a cell at 2 pm on a weekday and hear what a homeowner gets. If it's voicemail, change the greeting to promise a text back within 15 minutes, and keep that promise. Plenty of homeowners would rather text anyway.
guesses.fix: Missed-call text-back from the phone feature in their CRM, or a business phone service if it doesn't have one. Every missed call gets an instant text ("Sorry we missed you, we're on a roof. What's the address and what's going on?"), and the reply lands in the lead inbox with a callback task.

guesses.ask: How many supplements are sitting open right now?
guesses.label: Supplements sitting open
guesses.tip: The lines that get missed most are code items: drip edge, ice and water at the eaves, starter, steep and high charges. Check the approved scope against local code before tear-off, and cite the code section with photos in the supplement. A code citation is hard for an adjuster to argue with.
guesses.fix: Each open supplement is a line on the job's money-owed list with the amount and the date sent, plus a follow-up date that brings it back every 7 days until it's approved or denied. If they'd rather not do supplements in-house, a supplement service paid on a percentage of what it recovers needs no staff. The board just tracks what was sent.

guesses.ask: Any mortgage-company checks waiting on signatures?
guesses.label: Mortgage checks stuck
guesses.tip: Get the loan number and the lender's loss-draft department number at contract signing, not when the check shows up. Loss-draft departments usually want the endorsed check, the signed contract, a W-9 and often an inspection request. Send the whole packet at once instead of finding out one item at a time.
guesses.fix: Each mortgage check is its own line on the money-owed list (received, endorsed, sent to the lender, released), and the loss-draft packet is a saved checklist on the job. Anything sitting 7 days comes back as a call-the-lender task.

guesses.ask: Are you still the one meeting the adjusters, or do you have someone for that?
guesses.label: Owner does every adjuster meeting
guesses.tip: Record a voice memo of your next three adjuster meetings, start to finish. A new rep learns more from hearing how you walk an adjuster through the damage than from any checklist you could write.
guesses.fix: An adjuster playbook built from the owner's own recordings, plus a required-photo checklist in CompanyCam so every rep documents the same way. Adjuster meetings go on a rep's calendar, and the owner only takes the hard ones.

guesses.ask: Are your crews in-house or subs?
guesses.label: Sub crews are hard to coordinate
guesses.tip: Send subs one link per job (a CompanyCam project or shared album) instead of a text thread: address, scope, material order, gate code and the inspection photos. Ask for the done photos in the same link. Subs actually like this one, because it ends the 9 pm calls.
guesses.fix: One CompanyCam project per job is the sub's whole world: address, scope, material order, gate code, and the done photos go back in the same place. The night-before text comes from the schedule if the CRM can send it, or from a saved template. Subs never open the CRM.

guesses.ask: You've probably still got a backlog to finish before the snow, right?
guesses.label: Racing the snow / backlog
guesses.tip: Rank the backlog by money already out: jobs with materials delivered or ACV checks cashed go first, because that's your money sitting in someone's driveway. And check each manufacturer's cold-weather instructions before pushing into December. Seal strips don't bond in the cold without hand-sealing.
guesses.fix: The board sorted by money at risk (materials delivered, ACV check cashed) becomes the build order. Weather calls stay a human decision; the new-date text to the homeowner is a saved template, one tap.

guesses.ask: How many "when's my roof going on" calls do you get in a week?
guesses.label: Lots of "when's my roof" calls
guesses.tip: Those calls aren't about the roof. They're about not knowing when they'll hear from you next. End every homeowner call with a date: "You'll hear from me Thursday either way." Then call Thursday.
guesses.fix: The CRM's built-in customer texts go out every time the job changes stage: claim approved, materials ordered, install date, crew on site, final walkthrough. Nobody types anything new.

guesses.ask: When you sell an upgraded manufacturer warranty, who registers it, and when?
guesses.label: Warranties not registered
guesses.tip: Pick ten jobs from last year and look them up in the manufacturer's contractor portal. Enhanced warranties have to be registered within a set window after install. If one got missed, the homeowner doesn't have the warranty you sold them, and it's better you find that out than they do.
guesses.fix: Moving a job to Paid creates a "register the warranty" task with the deadline. It stays on the board until it's done.

guesses.ask: When hail hits a neighborhood you've already roofed, do your past customers hear from you before the door-knockers show up?
guesses.label: Past customers not contacted after storms
guesses.tip: Your past customers and their neighbors are your warmest leads after a storm. Keep every roof you've done listed by zip code, and text that zip the morning after hail with a free re-inspection offer. It beats knocking cold doors.
guesses.fix: Every past job is in the CRM with its address. The morning after hail, the office filters by zip code and sends one saved text with a free re-inspection offer. Replies land in the lead inbox.

guesses.ask: How do you ask for reviews? Is it automatic, or when someone remembers?
guesses.label: Reviews not asked for consistently
guesses.tip: Ask in person at the final walkthrough while the crew is cleaning up, then text the direct write-a-review link before you leave the driveway. Use the link that opens the review form, not your Google listing. It saves them three taps.
guesses.fix: When the final payment comes in, the CRM's built-in review request texts the direct Google link, with one reminder 3 days later.

guesses.ask: When the crew finds rotten decking on tear-off, how does that get approved and billed?
guesses.label: Field extras not billed
guesses.tip: Put the per-sheet decking price in the contract, and have the crew lead photograph every bad sheet before it's replaced, with a count. Then it's a line on the invoice instead of an argument, and on insurance jobs the photos go straight into the supplement.
guesses.fix: An extra-decking checklist in CompanyCam with required photos and a sheet count. The office adds the line to the invoice (or the supplement) the same day, at the per-sheet price in the contract. The crew keeps doing what they already do: take photos.

guess.why: Read their size first. Under 30 reviews: the owner does everything, so talk about their time. 30–150: owner plus one overloaded office person, your sweet spot. 150+: managers and software, so ask for operations. Ask one guess, then stop talking. If they say yes, tag it, give the free tip, and save the fix for the audit. If you're wrong: "Oh, interesting, how do you handle that?"

paths.label: None fit: ask how they handle it
Plenty there: bridge to the close

no-lead-tracking.label: Leads not tracked anywhere central
no-lead-tracking.tip: put every new lead in one shared list with a next step and a date, and review it for 10 minutes every Monday.

rep-owned-leads.label: Leads live in reps' phones
rep-owned-leads.tip: put every new lead in one shared list with a next step and a date, and review it for 10 minutes every Monday.

storm-lead-overload.label: Storm leads pile up faster than you can work them
storm-lead-overload.tip: after a storm, sort every lead into today / this week / later on day one, and call the today pile before you knock another door.

slow-lead-response.label: Slow speed-to-lead
slow-lead-response.tip: set up an instant auto-text to every new lead saying you'll call within the hour, and make same-hour callbacks a rule.

slow-estimates.label: Estimates take days to get out
slow-estimates.tip: order the aerial measurement report the moment the inspection is booked, so the numbers are ready when you leave the roof.

no-estimate-followup.label: Unsigned estimates go cold
no-estimate-followup.tip: follow up every unsigned estimate on day 2, day 5 and day 10. Even a calendar reminder for each one wins deals back.

inconsistent-followup.label: Follow-up depends on the rep
inconsistent-followup.tip: follow up every unsigned estimate on day 2, day 5 and day 10. Even a calendar reminder for each one wins deals back.

pipeline-spreadsheet.label: Jobs tracked on a spreadsheet or whiteboard
pipeline-spreadsheet.tip: add a stage and a days-in-stage column to your job list and sort by days-in-stage every Monday. The stuck jobs jump right out.

key-person-risk.label: Job status lives in one person's head
key-person-risk.tip: add a stage and a days-in-stage column to your job list and sort by days-in-stage every Monday. The stuck jobs jump right out.

fragmented-tools.label: Job status split across tools
fragmented-tools.tip: pick one place where every job's stage lives, and update it before you text anyone about the job.

insurance-delays.label: Jobs stuck waiting on insurance / adjusters
insurance-delays.tip: log the date of every claim and adjuster meeting, and set a follow-up reminder every 5 business days until approval.

unfiled-supplements.label: Supplements not filed or not chased
unfiled-supplements.tip: check every approved scope against what you actually installed before the final invoice, and file the supplement that same week.

material-delays.label: Waiting on material deliveries
material-delays.tip: confirm the material drop with the supplier 48 hours out, and don't lock the crew until it's confirmed.

weather-backlog.label: Weather reschedules snowball
weather-backlog.tip: keep a ranked 'next up if it's dry' list, so a rain day reshuffles in five minutes instead of an afternoon.

no-pipeline-visibility.label: No clear count of stalled jobs
no-pipeline-visibility.tip: add a stage and a days-in-stage column to your job list and sort by days-in-stage every Monday. The stuck jobs jump right out.

delayed-cash.label: Stalled jobs delay cash flow
delayed-cash.tip: add a money-still-owed column to every job and review it every Friday.

uncollected-depreciation.label: Depreciation checks left uncollected
uncollected-depreciation.tip: send the completion paperwork to the carrier the day the roof is done, and keep a list of every job with depreciation still owed.

mortgage-checks.label: Checks stuck with mortgage companies
mortgage-checks.tip: keep a list of which mortgage companies hold each check, what they need to release it, and when you last called.

deductible-chasing.label: Chasing deductibles / final invoices
deductible-chasing.tip: collect the deductible at the start of the job, not the end, and put the final-payment date in writing when they sign.

payments-spreadsheet.label: Money owed tracked in a spreadsheet
payments-spreadsheet.tip: add a money-still-owed column to every job and review it every Friday.

manual-status-updates.label: Status updates done by hand
manual-status-updates.tip: text every homeowner when their job changes stage. Even a template you send by hand cuts most of the 'when's my roof' calls.

reactive-comms.label: Homeowners have to call for updates
reactive-comms.tip: text every homeowner when their job changes stage. Even a template you send by hand cuts most of the 'when's my roof' calls.

rep-as-support.label: Sales reps stuck doing customer support
rep-as-support.tip: text every homeowner when their job changes stage, so the rep isn't the only one who knows.

whens-my-roof.label: Constant "when's my roof getting done?" calls
whens-my-roof.tip: text every homeowner when their job changes stage. Even a template you send by hand cuts most of the 'when's my roof' calls.

bad-reviews.label: Delays hurting reviews / cancellations
bad-reviews.tip: text every homeowner when their job changes stage. Silence is what turns into a bad review.

manual-scheduling.label: Scheduling on whiteboard / group text
manual-scheduling.tip: put every crew and every job on one shared calendar that everyone can see, even if it's just a Google Calendar.

owner-scheduling.label: Owner is the scheduling bottleneck
owner-scheduling.tip: write down how you decide which crew gets which job, then hand the easy 80% to the office.

sub-coordination.label: Coordinating subcontracted crews
sub-coordination.tip: send every sub the same job sheet (address, materials, photos, special notes) the day before, every time.

wasted-trips.label: Wasted trips / crew shows up and can't start
wasted-trips.tip: do a ready-check call 48 hours before every job: materials dropped, dumpster set, homeowner confirmed.

double-bookings.label: Double-booked crews
double-bookings.tip: put every crew and every job on one shared calendar that everyone can see.

manual-commissions.label: Commissions calculated by hand
manual-commissions.tip: write the commission rules on one page and send each rep a per-job statement when the job is paid in full.

commission-disputes.label: Commission disputes with reps
commission-disputes.tip: write the commission rules on one page and send each rep a per-job statement when the job is paid in full.

photos-only.label: Photo app, but no job management

generic-fsm.label: Generic field-service tool, not built for roofing

double-entry.label: Re-typing data between tools
double-entry.tip: pick one system as the source of truth for customer info, and enter it there first, every time.

owner-admin.label: Owner buried in admin / insurance paperwork

missed-calls.label: Missed calls while crews are on roofs
missed-calls.tip: change the voicemail greeting to promise a text back within 15 minutes, and keep the promise.

warranty-not-registered.label: Manufacturer warranties not registered
warranty-not-registered.tip: look up last year's jobs in the manufacturer's contractor portal. An unregistered enhanced warranty is one you sold that the homeowner doesn't have.

past-customers-ignored.label: Past customers not contacted after storms
past-customers-ignored.tip: keep every roof you've done listed by zip code, and text that zip the morning after hail with a free re-inspection offer.

no-review-requests.label: Reviews not asked for consistently
no-review-requests.tip: ask in person at the final walkthrough, then text the direct write-a-review link before you leave the driveway.

unbilled-change-orders.label: Extra decking / field extras not billed
unbilled-change-orders.tip: put the per-sheet decking price in the contract, and photograph every bad sheet before it's replaced.

learn_q1.question: Question 1: how do you track money still owed?
learn_q1.say: First one: when a job's waiting on insurance, a supplement or a depreciation check, how do you keep track of it?
learn_q1.why: Whatever they say, follow with 'how's that working for you?' If they open up, hit Go deeper.

answers.label: In my head / my foreman's head

opener.question: Permission-based intro
say: Hey, this is {{me}}. I'll be quick, and this is a cold call, so feel free to hang up on me in 30 seconds.
Mind if I take 30 seconds to tell you why I called, and you tell me if it's worth talking?
opener.why: Saying it's a cold call and asking permission lowers their guard. They get to say yes.

answers.label: Who is this? What's it about?

opener_pitch.question: Reason for the call, ending in a problem question
say: The reason I'm calling: I work with {{trade}} around Denver on the operations side, from the signed contract to the last check.

Something a lot of insurance roofers deal with is money sitting on the table: depreciation checks nobody chased, supplements that never got filed, final invoices that drag on because the job status lives in someone's head.
Is that something you run into, or do you have that pretty buttoned up?
opener_pitch.why: State the reason in one breath, name a problem they'll recognize, and end on a question they can answer either way. Uncollected money is the sharpest pain in insurance roofing. Lead with it.

opener_buttoned.question: "We're buttoned up": check the front end
say: Shops that have production dialed in usually still lose deals on the front end, especially after a storm, when leads pile up and estimates don't get a follow-up.
opener_buttoned.why: 'Buttoned up' on one side usually means the problem is somewhere else. Check the other half of the business before you move on.

opener_gatekeeper.question: Find the right person
say: No worries. I'm trying to reach whoever handles how jobs and scheduling work there. Is that the owner or someone else?
When's the best time to catch them?
opener_gatekeeper.why: Get a name and a time. Write both in Notes.

answers.label: Got a name and a time, log a callback

opener_voicemail.question: Voicemail (under 20 seconds)
say: Hi {{contact|there}}, {{me}} here. I help {{trade}} in Denver collect the money that slips through on insurance jobs: depreciation, supplements, final invoices.
I had one specific idea for {{business|your company}}. I'm at [your number]. Again, [your number]. Thanks.
opener_voicemail.why: Follow up in 2 business days. Try 3 times max before moving on.

answers.label: Left it, log a follow-up in 2 days

pipeline_tracking.question: How do you track a job from signed to paid?
pipeline_tracking.say: Once a homeowner signs, there's the claim, the adjuster, approval, materials, the install, and getting paid. How do you keep track of where every job is?
pipeline_tracking.why: This is the core of the audit. When the work moves but the status doesn't, money gets left behind.

answers.label: Office manager keeps it in their head

pipeline_stuck.question: Where do jobs sit the longest?
pipeline_stuck.say: Out of all those steps, where do jobs tend to sit the longest?
pipeline_stuck.why: Every stalled week pushes back the final check. Find out which step stalls and you know where to start.

pipeline_count.question: How many jobs are stalled right now?
pipeline_count.say: If I asked you right now how many jobs are open, and how many are stalled, could you tell me?
pipeline_count.why: Not knowing this number off the top of their head is the 'owner dashboard' problem.

pipeline_impact.question: What does a stalled job cost you?
pipeline_impact.say: When a job sits stuck for a few extra weeks, what does that do on your end?
pipeline_impact.why: This is the implication question: it turns a process problem into money and stress. If they light up, open Go deeper and get a number.

answers.label: I end up chasing it myself

money_collect.question: How do you track money still owed on each job?
money_collect.say: How do you keep track of what's still owed on each job: deductibles, depreciation, supplements, the final invoice?
money_collect.why: This is where roofers leave the most money behind, and nobody notices because nothing went 'wrong'. If they hesitate, go deeper.

answers.label: Tracked in our software, it's tight

money_leak.question: How much is out there right now?
money_leak.say: If you added up every depreciation check, supplement and final payment still out there right now, do you know roughly what that number is?
money_leak.why: If they know it, write it in Go deeper. That's their cost. If they don't, not knowing is the pain.

money_commissions.question: How are rep commissions handled?
money_commissions.say: And sales rep commissions: how do those get calculated and paid out?
money_commissions.why: Commission disputes take up the owner's time and drive good reps away, and storm reps leave fast.

comms_updates.question: How do homeowners get status updates?
comms_updates.say: While all that's happening, how does the homeowner find out where their job is at, especially while they're waiting on insurance?
comms_updates.why: Homeowners waiting on insurance feel stuck. If they hear nothing, they call, leave bad reviews, or sign with the next guy who knocks.

comms_calls.question: How many "when's my roof getting done?" calls a week?
comms_calls.say: Roughly how many "when's my roof getting done?" calls or texts do you get in a week?
comms_calls.why: Each one is someone stopping what they're doing to look up a job's status by hand.

crew_scheduling.question: How do jobs get on the calendar?
crew_scheduling.say: How do jobs get scheduled, and what happens to the schedule when the weather turns?
crew_scheduling.why: In Colorado the weather reshuffles the schedule every week. If the owner is the only one who can rebuild it, the owner is the bottleneck.

crew_problems.question: Wasted trips or double-bookings?
crew_problems.say: In the last month, any wasted trips? A crew shows up and the materials, the dumpster or the homeowner isn't ready?
crew_problems.why: A wasted trip costs a crew-day. Owners remember these, so ask for a specific story.

tools_current.question: What software runs the business today?
tools_current.say: What are you using to run all this today, software-wise?
tools_current.why: Write the exact tool names in Notes. You'll need them for the audit and the build.

tools_fit.question: Do the tools talk to each other?
tools_fit.say: Do those tools talk to each other, or is someone re-typing the same info from one into another?
tools_fit.why: Re-typing data between tools is a quick fix that's easy to show results on.

answers.label: Paying for stuff we don't use

owner_week.question: What eats most of your week?
owner_week.say: Last one, the big one: what eats most of your week?
owner_week.why: This is the pain they feel personally. Write down their exact words, because you'll repeat them in the close.

answers.label: Chasing job status / putting out fires

owner_one_thing.question: If one thing ran itself, what would you pick?
owner_one_thing.say: If one thing in the business just ran itself, what would you pick?
owner_one_thing.why: Their answer is what you sell the audit on. It shows up at the top of the pain summary.

lead_source.question: Where do most of your leads come from?
lead_source.say: Where do most of your new jobs come from right now: storm canvassing, referrals, Google, lead services?
lead_source.why: After a hailstorm every roofer in town is calling the same homeowners. Whoever follows up first and stays organized wins.

lead_tracking.question: How are leads tracked, especially after a storm?
lead_tracking.say: When a storm hits and the leads pour in, where do they all go? How do you keep track?
lead_tracking.why: Storm leads are perishable. If they live in reps' phones, you can't see what's falling through, and they leave when the rep leaves.

lead_speed.question: How fast does a new lead get a call back?
lead_speed.say: And when a new lead comes in, how fast does someone usually get back to them?
lead_speed.why: Leads called back within minutes convert far better than next-day callbacks. This is often the cheapest fix there is.

sales_proposal.question: How do estimates get built?
sales_proposal.say: After an inspection, how does the estimate get put together, and how long does that usually take?
sales_proposal.why: The homeowner is getting three bids. A slow estimate loses to a fast one.

answers.label: By hand after the roof climb
Mostly insurance scope, we match it

sales_followup.question: What happens to unsigned estimates?
sales_followup.say: Quick question: when you send an estimate and don't hear back, what happens next?
sales_followup.why: Stop talking after you ask. "Nothing" or "I try to remember" is the pain.

answers.label: Rep follows up when they remember

sales_close_rate.question: Rough close rate?
sales_close_rate.say: Roughly what share of the estimates you send end up signing?
sales_close_rate.why: If they don't know this number, nobody is watching the funnel.
